blocks.text: Show history through seams. Era overlap should appear as patched thresholds, mismatched scale, preserved anchor objects, and functions reused by later peoples.
Corruption should mean something. Repetition may come from recurrence; blankness from deletion; pale uniformity from standardization; overlap from world folding; misnamed weather from semantic drift.
Protect body scale. Era Three spaces should show how small bodies inhabit DBA structures: ledges become roads, doors become squares, vents become weather, interface recesses become wells.

Keep the foreground playable. For a 480 × 360 background, reserve a clear walking surface and horizon. Put the most complex historical evidence in middle and far layers unless the location’s friction is the point.

Use motion as memory. Small loops can communicate lost function: lights answering in sequence, a route repairing itself, a branch displaying another room, a wave returning the wrong artifact, or an unanswered festival setup.

Do not depict DBA persons as secretly intact pets. Ancient voices, silhouettes, or images are records, temporary reconstructions, environmental responses, myths, or uncertain residues unless canon explicitly establishes otherwise.
Do not insert humans into Era Three. Human-origin imagery may survive in archives and translations, but living human contact resumes only at the beginning of Era Four.

Preserve ordinary value. A place does not need a player to become meaningful. Nests, meals, markets, repeated games, local celebrations, healing, and care are already lives of value. External participation permits further transformation.
